patient_note_history:
History:
HPI: A 28-year-old female complains of pain during intercourse for 3 months. The pain is located both externally and internally with deep thrusting. She also noticed a scant, white vaginal discharge with a fishy odor, accompanied by mild vaginal pruritus. She denies postcoital or intermenstrual vaginal bleeding. She is sexually active with her boyfriend for the past year and denies concerns regarding her desire for sexual activity. She denies any conflicts with her partner. She also denies vaginal dryness, hot flashes, depression, and urinary frequency. 
OB/GYN: Gynecological/Obstetric: Gravida, para, and abortions all zero (GOPO). LMP 2 weeks ago; has regular menses but started to have pain with menses over the past year. No history of abnormal Pap smears; the most recent one was 6 months ago. Uses patch for contraception. 
ROS: Negative except as above.
NKDA.
Medications: No, I have not. 
PMH: History of rape 10 years ago; subsequently contracted gonorrhea.
PSH: No, I have not. 
SH: No tobacco. Occasional alcohol intake. Exercises regularly.

gold_additional_diagnosis:
• Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID): The patient's history of gonorrhea infection (if it caused PID) also puts her at risk for pelvic scarring and subsequent dyspareunia (due to adhesions resulting in impaired mobility of the pelvic organs).
• Vulvodynia: This is the leading cause of dyspareunia in premenopausal women, but it is not well understood. Pain may be constant or intermittent, focal or diffuse, and superficial or deep and may or may not be related to sexual activity. Physical findings are often absent, making it a diagnosis of exclusion. Vulvar erythema can be seen in a subset of vulvodynia termed vulvar vestibulitis.
• Domestic violence: Physicians must screen for this in any woman presenting with dyspareunia. Serial screening is required as victims may not disclose this history initially.
• Pelvic tumor: This could account for the patient's pain with deep thrusting and possibly for her history of dysmenorrhea. However, pelvic tumors are not associated with vaginal discharge and pruritus.
• Vaginismus: This describes severe involuntary spasm of muscles around the introitus and often results from fear, pain, or sexual or psychological trauma. The muscle contractions generally preclude penetration. This patient does not describe the muscle contractions characteristic of vaginismus.
